title: Not me, us: a system for climate refugee prediction and resettlement

context_sources.name: Feng S, disappearance of the state under sea level rise, Modern Law Science, 2019
IPCC report, temperature and sea level
Chen, Chen and Xiu, network-flow model of the European refugee crisis, 2016

limitations: A watermark replaces operators and digits across the regression, cost, incentive and shelter formulas.
The appendix prints a second stress-weight vector that contradicts the prose.
The summary's 3.43 billion dollar bill does not match the case arithmetic.
The comparison matrices are promised for an appendix that the text does not contain.

tasks: Forecast the rise and the displaced population
Rank hosts by natural and cultural match
Cap intake by an electorally calibrated stress line
Schedule the move and split the bill by emissions
Place people temporarily after a sudden shock

section_map.summary: Six-part system, Maldives to Malaysia in 2044, Japan shock to three neighbors.
Slow case and sudden case, each routed through the same payer.
No persecutor, so old conventions fail. Three principles.
Differenced regression, circular land, three-part cultural loss.
Hierarchy, stress index, program, cost share, temporary shelter.
Two scenarios, one or two hosts, G20 bill.
Half the population, cap raised, China, Russia, South Korea.
Law of state disappearance, altimetry data, a refugee network-flow model.

contributions.summary: A stress index whose refusal line is read off three elections rather than chosen.
An emission share reduced by the geometric mean of recent per-person cuts.
A capped greedy fill for emergency shelter, with the overflow reallocated by score.

dependency_graph.handoff: The dated headcount and the deadline come from the sea-level projection
The cultural loss figure enters the bill as the protection base
Host match scores become the welfare weights
The stress line caps each host's yearly intake
The resulting headcount and treatment level set the per-person cost
After the emergency, the same scheduling model places people permanently

assumptions.summary: Altitude is negligible against a territory's width, so land is a flat circle.
Half the world population lives within 150 km of a coast.
Voters force a refusal once stress crosses one world threshold.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Temperature and sea level from the IPCC report, differenced after a stationarity test.
World Bank forecasts, Phillips curve and Okun's law for prices and jobs, Monte Carlo for crises and crime.

models.summary: Differenced quadratic regression plus a ring-flood population count.
Three-carrier cultural valuation with country-specific weights.
Eight-indicator hierarchy with a consistency gate.
Five-indicator stress index with a squared refugee share.
Monotone welfare program solved in two steps.
Treatment cost plus culture protection, shared by incentivized emissions.
Three-indicator emergency shelter score with a population cap.

verification.summary: Maldives hierarchy passes with a consistency ratio of 0.0068.
The stress line is checked against three election years.

results_trace.summary: Maldives: 0.67 m by 2035, 1.44 m at one degree of warming, uninhabitable mid-century.
Malaysia alone over seven years, or Malaysia plus India inside five, 70 to 80 thousand a year.
A Japan shock sends half the population to China, Russia and South Korea.

writing_logic.summary: The sudden case is defined as what happens when the slow process has no time.
A threshold is derived from elections, then shifted for the lag between mood and vote.
Monotonicity is stated first so the two-step solve looks forced.

language_observations.summary: A legal gap opened by the absence of a persecutor.
A named election used as the mechanism behind a model threshold.
A square term justified by disgust rising faster than gains.
The emergency's scarce resource identified as preparation time, not willingness.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: the emergency path from shock to temporary shelter to a lasting home.
Figure 2: the problem restated as a diagram of questions.
Figure 3: land drawn as a circle with a flooded ring.
Figure 4: the broker, the hosts, and the payers.
Figure 5: the hierarchy diagram. A second Figure 5 later shows the shelter algorithm.
Figure 6: stress in three countries from 2008 to 2018.
Figure 7: the Maldives, landscape and location.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Calibrating the refusal line on real elections makes the cap arguable rather than arbitrary.
Rewarding recent cuts stops the cost share from being pure backward-looking blame.
Showing that delay drags in a worse-matched host gives the lead time a reason.

weaknesses.summary: The stated bill of 3.43 billion dollars conflicts with the case arithmetic.
The prose and the appendix code give different stress weights.
The shelter weights are cited but not legible, so the Japan ranking cannot be checked.

independent_extensions.summary: Recompute the Maldives bill from the stated unit cost and settle which total is intended.
Decide between the prose weights and the appendix weights and rerun the stress index.
Publish the comparison matrices behind the Maldives ranking.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Set a host's intake limit from observed political breaking points, not from a round number.
Split a climate bill by past emissions but reduce it for states that have already cut.

unresolved_questions.question: Is the Maldives bill 3.43 billion dollars or the much larger case-text figure?
Which stress weights were used, the prose set or the code set?
What weight triple produced the Japan shelter ranking?
